title: The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings

hero.subtitle: Encoding binary data as printable ASCII text

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Base encodings convert arbitrary binary data into text using a restricted alphabet of printable ASCII characters. This is essential for transporting binary data through text-only channels such as email, URLs, and JSON.

Base64 is by far the most commonly used encoding. You encounter it in email attachments (MIME), data URIs, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), HTTP Basic authentication, and embedded images in CSS/HTML.

sections.title: Base64 Encoding
sections.content:
Base64 encoding groups input bytes into 24-bit blocks (3 bytes), then splits each block into four 6-bit groups. Each 6-bit value indexes into the Base64 alphabet to produce a printable character.

Base64 Alphabet
Value  Char   Value  Char   Value  Char   Value  Char
  0    A       16    Q       32    g       48    w
  1    B       17    R       33    h       49    x
  2    C       18    S       34    i       50    y
  3    D       19    T       35    j       51    z
  4    E       20    U       36    k       52    0
  5    F       21    V       37    l       53    1
  ...  ...     ...   ...     ...   ...     ...   ...
 25    Z       41    p       51    z       63    /
                                        (pad)   =
Encoding Example: "Man"
Text:    M           a           n
ASCII:   77          97          110
Binary:  01001101    01100001    01101110

6-bit:   010011  010110  000101  101110
Value:   19      22      5       46
Base64:  T       W       F       u

Result: "Man" -> "TWFu"

sections.title: Base32 Encoding
sections.content:
Base32 uses a 32-character alphabet (A-Z and 2-7) and groups data into 5-bit chunks. It is less space-efficient than Base64 but uses only uppercase letters and digits, making it suitable for case-insensitive contexts.

sections.title: Base16 (Hex) Encoding
sections.content:
Base16 uses the hexadecimal digits 0-9 and A-F. Each byte is represented by exactly two hex characters. While it doubles the data size, it provides direct byte-level inspection.

Base16 Examples
"Hello" -> 48656C6C6F
"Man"   -> 4D616E
\x00    -> 00
\xff    -> FF

Base16 is commonly used for displaying cryptographic hashes (SHA-256, MD5), MAC addresses (00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E), and debugging binary protocols. It is case-insensitive per this specification.

sections.title: Padding
sections.content:
When the input length is not evenly divisible by the group size, padding characters (=) are appended to the output.

Base64, 0 remainingNo padding needed
Base64, 1 remainingTwo = characters appended
Base64, 2 remainingOne = character appended
Padding Examples
"Man"    -> "TWFu"     (3 bytes = no padding)
"Ma"     -> "TWE="     (2 bytes = 1 pad)
"M"      -> "TQ=="     (1 byte  = 2 pads)

sections.title: URL-Safe Base64 Variant
sections.content:
The standard Base64 alphabet includes + and / which have special meaning in URLs. The URL-safe variant (base64url) replaces these characters.

+ replaced by -Plus sign is replaced with hyphen/minusIndex 62
/ replaced by _Forward slash is replaced with underscoreIndex 63

The base64url encoding is required by several modern standards including JSON Web Tokens (JWT/JWS/JWE), OAuth 2.0 PKCE, and data URIs. Padding may be omitted in contexts where the data length is known.
